statement: The paper's ITL = alpha/(1-rho) formula achieves MAPE < 0.1% at low rates (5-20 req/s) in BLIS finite-horizon simulations (300 requests), confirming quantitative accuracy in the steady-state regime.
regime: 300-request finite-horizon simulation at rates 5-20 req/s; simulation duration >> service time (duration/service_time >= 9)
mechanism: At low rates, the 300-request simulation duration (60s at rate=5, 15s at rate=20) is long enough for the batch to reach approximate steady-state. The positive feedback loop (larger batch -> slower iterations -> even larger batch) has time to fully engage, and the remaining simulation time is dominated by near-steady-state behavior. The formula's two free parameters (alpha, w) can be calibrated from any two low-rate observations.
applicability_bounds: Applies when simulation duration / per-request service time >= ~9. Breaks down when this ratio < ~2 (rates >= 100 req/s in the 300-request setup). Formula is structurally correct; breakdown is purely a finite-horizon effect.

statement: A simple linear fit (ITL = a + b*rate) achieves R² > 0.975 across rates 5-150 req/s for both AL and AD modes in 300-request finite-horizon BLIS simulations, outperforming the best-fit 1/(1-rho) formula (R² < 0.95).
regime: 300-request finite-horizon simulations; rates 5-150 req/s; 4-instance cluster with 2 prefill, 2 decode; fixed token lengths (512+128=640 tokens)
mechanism: In the finite-horizon regime, the mean batch size grows approximately linearly with rate (batch never reaches the 1/(1-rho) steady-state size), producing an approximately linear ITL-vs-rate relationship. The paper's formula is convex (accelerating growth), but the observed data is concave (decelerating growth) because the transient ramp-up limits how large the batch grows before all 300 requests complete.
applicability_bounds: Holds for 300-request simulations at rates 5-150. Expected to fail for very long simulations (>>1000 requests at high rates) where steady-state is reached. The linear approximation is an artifact of the finite-horizon regime, not a correction to the paper's formula.

statement: The formula overprediction percentage (calibrated 1/(1-rho) vs observed ITL) is strictly monotone increasing with arrival rate for rates >= 20 req/s, reaching 108% for AL and 50% for AD at rate=150 req/s.
regime: Low-rate calibration (rates 5, 10 as calibration points); extrapolation to rates 20-150; 300-request simulation
mechanism: As rate increases, the ratio (experiment duration / service time) decreases monotonically, meaning the fraction of simulation time spent in transient (non-steady-state) behavior increases monotonically. The formula assumes steady-state batch size, so its overprediction grows monotonically. AL overpredicts more than AD because w_AL > w_AD (0.00471 vs 0.00369), making the formula's denominator (1-rate*w) smaller for AL, amplifying the convexity mismatch.
applicability_bounds: Holds for two-point calibration at (5,10) with extrapolation to higher rates. Would not apply if calibrating at higher rates.

statement: The two-point calibrated formula parameters confirm w_AL > w_AD (0.00471 vs 0.00369), consistent with the paper's prediction that Always-Local mode incurs more per-request processing work than Always-Disaggregate decode-only mode.
regime: 4-instance cluster (2 prefill, 2 decode); fixed 512+128 token lengths; rates 5-150 req/s
mechanism: In AL mode, each decode instance handles both prefill and decode phases for each request. In AD mode, prefill instances handle the compute-intensive prefill phase and decode instances handle only the decode phase (pure batch decode at alpha_D < alpha_total). The reduced per-instance work in AD mode means each decode token takes less time (smaller effective alpha_D), so the formula parameter w_AD (which captures the time each request occupies the system per token) is smaller than w_AL.
applicability_bounds: Quantitative values (0.00471 vs 0.00369) are specific to qwen3-14b, 4-instance cluster, 512+128 tokens. The directional inequality (w_AL > w_AD) should hold generally whenever AL processing is compute-heavier than AD decode-only processing.
